sentences: On the roof of a small school, a weather station quietly records changes in the air throughout the day and night.
The students helped choose its position, away from tall walls and warm air rising from the building's ventilation system.
A shallow container measures rainfall, while another instrument records the direction and strength of the wind above the playground.
Every morning, a different pair of students checks the equipment and compares the latest readings with the notes from the previous day.
They soon discover that a single measurement tells only a small part of the story, especially when the weather is changing quickly.
One bright afternoon can follow a week of heavy rain, and a cold morning does not necessarily mean that the whole month has been cold.
The science teacher encourages the class to look for patterns without pretending that every unusual number must have an exciting explanation.
Sometimes a bird has landed on a sensor, or a loose connection has interrupted the stream of information reaching the classroom computer.
Those gaps are written down instead of being filled with invented readings, so that anyone using the records later can understand what happened.
After six months, the class shares a short report with a nearby garden whose volunteers want to plan their watering more carefully.
The volunteers explain which details are useful to them and suggest adding a simple description of the soil after each period of rain.
What began as a lesson about instruments becomes a lesson about asking good questions, checking evidence, and making information useful to other people.
At the end of the school year, the older students teach the next class how to maintain the station and keep its notebook organized.
The equipment remains on the roof during the holidays, ready to continue a record that will become more valuable as the years pass.
